> ## 2. How a client proves identity
> 
> Two mechanisms; **no passwords anywhere**. Identity **is a phone number** (`users.md:13`: *"Identity is a phone number"*).
> 
> ### (a) SMS PIN (bootstrap + recovery)
> 
> `features/miso/users/pin/pin.rs`:
> ```
> 11:    fn make_pin() -&gt; String {
> 12:        let b = random_bytes(2);
> 13:        let n = ((b[0] as u32) * 256 + (b[1] as u32)) % 10000;
> 14:        format!("{:04}", n)
> ```
> **4 digits, and derived by `% 10000` from a 16-bit value — modulo-biased** (values 0–5535 are ~2× as likely as 5536–9999).
> 
> ```
> 46:        set_pending_line(phone, format!("{} {} 0", pin, now_ms() + 300000));   // 5-min TTL
> 102:        if sms_count_last_hour(phone.clone()) &gt;= 5 {                          // 5 SMS/phone/hour
> 143:        if attempts + 1 &gt; 3 {                                                 // 3 attempts
> 148:        if !constant_eq(want.clone(), pin) {
> ```
> Attempt counter is **per pending PIN**, and there is **no rate limit on `auth/verify` itself** — only the 3-attempt counter and the 5-req/hour ceiling on `auth/request`. 5 codes/hr × 3 guesses = 15 guesses/hr against a 10 000-space.
> 
> Guest-list precheck leaks membership:
> ```
> 96:        if name.is_empty() {
> 98:            return json_response(403, "...that number isn't on the guest list...")
> ```
> → a phone-number oracle for the guest list.
> 
> Pending PINs are **plaintext on disk**: `~/.miso-auth/pending.txt`, `"&lt;phone&gt; &lt;pin&gt; &lt;expiry&gt; &lt;attempts&gt;"` (`pin.rs:19-51`).
> 
> ### (b) Passkey / WebAuthn (Face ID)
> 
> `features/miso/users/passkey/passkey.login.js:5-12` — `navigator.credentials.get`, `userVerification: "required"`. Registration (`enrol.login.js:11-19`) uses `alg: -7` (ES256), `residentKey: "required"`, `attestation: "none"` (so **no attestation validation at all** — the server trusts whatever public key it's handed).
> 
> Registration is cookie-gated (`passkey.rs:236-239, 249-252`); login is public by design.
>

> ## 3. How the server verifies
> 
> ### Session token — `features/miso/users/users.rs`
> 
> ```
> 103:    fn make_token(phone: String) -&gt; String {
> 104:        let exp = now_ms() + 31536000000u64;                    // 1 YEAR
> 105:        let payload = format!("{}.{}", phone.replace("+", ""), exp);
> 106:        format!("{}.{}", payload, hmac_sha256(secret(), payload.clone()))
> 107:    }
> 109:    fn token_valid(token: String) -&gt; bool {
> 110:        let parts: Vec&lt;&amp;str&gt; = token.split('.').collect();
> 111:        if parts.len() != 3 { return false; }
> 114:        let exp: u64 = parts[1].parse().unwrap_or(0);
> 115:        if exp &lt; now_ms() { return false; }
> 118:        let payload = format!("{}.{}", parts[0], parts[1]);
> 119:        constant_eq(hmac_sha256(secret(), payload), parts[2].to_string())
> ```
> Notable for red-teaming:
> - **Stateless, un-revocable.** `pin.rs:174` comments: *"stateless tokens can't be revoked server-side; logout clears the cookie"*. A stolen cookie is valid for a year; logout does nothing server-side. Only remediation is deleting `~/.miso-auth/secret`, which logs everyone out.
> - `token_phone` (`users.rs:133-140`) **re-derives the phone from `parts[0]` with no re-validation against the guest list on most paths** — it just prepends `+`. Removing someone from `users.json` does *not* invalidate their token; `auth_whoami` returns `name: ""` but `token_valid`/`authed`/`sender_of`/`context_user_of` all still say yes.
> - `constant_eq` (`users.rs:122-131`) short-circuits on **length mismatch** (fine for fixed-length hex) and compares hex strings, not bytes.
> - Cookie parse is naive: `users.rs:142-150` takes everything after `miso_auth=` to the next `;`.
> - HMAC-SHA256 is **hand-rolled** over `sha2` (`users.rs:73-92`) — ipad/opad construction looks correct, key &gt;64 hashed, resize to 64.
> 
> Cookie attributes (`pin.rs:158-160`, `passkey.rs:318-320`):
> ```
> "miso_auth={}; Max-Age=31536000; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax"
> ```
> `SameSite=Lax` + all state-changing endpoints are POST-with-JSON, so CSRF is mostly blocked, but **there is no CSRF token and no `Origin` check on `POST /msg`, `/auth/verify`, `/push/subscribe`, `/blackbox/events`**.
> 
> ### Passkey verification — `features/miso/users/passkey/passkey.rs`
> 
> ```
> 136:    fn client_data_challenge(client_data: Vec&lt;u8&gt;, expect_type: String) -&gt; String {
> 139:        if v["type"].as_str().unwrap_or("") != expect_type { return String::new(); }
> 142:        if v["origin"].as_str().unwrap_or("") != origin() { return String::new(); }
> 145:        v["challenge"].as_str().unwrap_or("").to_string()
> ```
> ```
> 303:        let auth_data = b64u_decode(v["auth_data"]...);
> 304:        if auth_data.len() &lt; 37
> 305:            || auth_data[0..32].to_vec() != sha256(rp_id().into_bytes())
> 306:            || auth_data[32] &amp; 0x05 != 0x05 {       // UP|UV flags
> 307:            return json_response(403, ... "verification failed" ...);
> 308:        }
> 309:        let mut msg = auth_data.clone();
> 310:        msg.extend(sha256(client_raw));
> 311:        let sig = b64u_decode(v["signature"]...);
> 312:        if !p256_verify(xy, msg, sig) {
> ```
> Checks present: type, origin (exact-string, hardcoded `https://miso.xn--nb-lkaa.org`, `passkey.rs:28-30`), rpIdHash, UP+UV flags, one-time challenge, ECDSA-P256-DER sig over `authData ‖ SHA256(clientDataJSON)`.
> 
> Gaps worth probing:
> - **No signature counter check** (`authData[33..37]` ignored) → cloned-authenticator detection absent.
> - The credential is looked up by attacker-supplied `id` **before** the challenge is consumed (`passkey.rs:287-291`) → unauthenticated credential-ID enumeration oracle (`"unknown passkey"` vs other errors).
> - **Login challenges are not bound to any user** (`passkey.rs:279`: `new_challenge("login", "-")`), and `take_challenge` returns `"-"`, checked only via `.is_empty()` (line 300). Any live login challenge works with any credential.
> - Challenge store is a flat file rewritten non-atomically (`passkey.rs:90-106`, `72-86`) — **TOCTOU / race: two concurrent requests can both consume the same challenge**, and concurrent writes can drop lines.
> - `parse_attested` (`passkey.rs:167-178`) does raw index arithmetic on attacker-controlled bytes; bounds are checked, but `unhex`/`hex_val` (49-64) silently map invalid nibbles to 0.
> 
> ### Route-chain gate — `features/miso/users/gate/gate.rs`
> 
> ```
> 25:        if !r.tunnel { return existing.route(r); }
> 28:        if authed(r.cookie.clone()) { return existing.route(r); }
> 31:        login_page()
> ```
> `r.tunnel` comes from `serve.rs:64-65`:
> ```
> 64:            if lower.starts_with("cf-connecting-ip:") {
> 65:                tunnel = true;
> ```
> **This is the single most attackable line.** Authorization is `!r.tunnel` → full bypass. Anyone who can reach port 8095 directly (LAN, or anything that reaches the mini without cloudflared) is unauthenticated-admin. And a client that sends a request *through* the tunnel can't strip the header (cloudflared always adds it), but any request arriving on 8095 from a non-tunnel path with no `cf-connecting-ip` is trusted completely. `messaging.rs:21-23`, `readout.rs:15-17`, `edit.rs:63`, `same-door.rs:14`, `alive.rs:51` all repeat the same `!r.tunnel || authed(...)` pattern.
> 
> Public allowlist (`gate/public/public.rs:6-16`) includes `path.starts_with("f/")` and `features/` — the whole feature tree is public.
> 
> `diag/report` is **fully unauthenticated by design** (`diag.rs:5-6`: *"public on purpose"*), 2 KB cap, appends to `/tmp/miso-diag.log` — an open log-injection/flooding surface (`\n` is stripped, line 20).

> ## 4. Where secrets live
> 
> From `deploy.md:37-42`:
> ```
> - `~/.miso-auth/`: guest list `users.json` (`_`-prefixed names are test users
>   whose PINs go to the log, no SMS), signing `secret`, `pending.txt`,
>   `passkeys.txt`, `push-subs.txt`, `challenges.txt`, `last-notified`.
> - `~/.agent-config.json`: Vonage credentials (shared with ftr).
> ```
> 
> - **Session signing key**: `users.rs:54-66` — 32 bytes from `/dev/urandom`, written with `std::fs::write` → **default 0644 permissions, no `chmod`**. Same for every other file in `~/.miso-auth/`.
> - **VAPID private key**: `push.rs:23-37`, `~/.miso-auth/vapid-secret`, same treatment.
> - **Vonage `api_key`/`api_secret`**: read from `~/.agent-config.json` and **passed on the `curl` argv** (`vonage.rs:21-22`) → visible in `ps` to any local user.
> - `random_bytes` (`users.rs:45-51`) ignores the result of `read_exact`: `let _ = f.read_exact(&amp;mut buf);` — a short read silently yields zero bytes.
> - Sensitive files are outside the deploy tree (deliberate — deploys can't wipe them), and `.gitignore` does not need to cover them.
> - Push payload plaintext is briefly written to `/tmp/miso-push-&lt;ms&gt;.bin` (`push.rs:158-159`), world-readable, predictable name.
> - `/tmp/miso-broadcast.json`, `/tmp/miso-diag.log`, `/tmp/miso-blackbox.log` are shared-world files.

> ## 6. Transport (per `deploy.md`)
> 
> - **The server itself speaks plain HTTP, stdlib only, port 8095, no TLS.** `serve.md:16`: *"using only the Rust standard library — no crates"*.
> - **TLS terminates at cloudflared**, a system daemon on the mini: `deploy.md:34-36` — *"Tunnel: cloudflared (system daemon, config `~/.cloudflared/config.yml`) maps `miso.xn--nb-lkaa.org` (= miso.nøøb.org) → localhost:8095"*.
> - The `Secure` cookie flag is therefore set on a cookie issued over cleartext HTTP inside the box; it survives only because the browser only ever sees the tunnel.
> - Outbound TLS (Vonage, Web Push) is delegated to `curl` subprocesses — `vonage.rs:5` comment: *"TLS is curl's problem, not ours."*
> - Host: `microserver@microservers-Mac-mini.local` on LAN, else `microserver@185.96.221.52`. Deploy is `rsync` + `launchctl kickstart` of LaunchAgent `com.noob.miso` (`deploy.md:22, 30-33`).
> - **Passkeys only work through the tunnel domain** — `rp_id` is hardcoded (`passkey.rs:24-26`).
>

> ## 7. Authorization (as opposed to authentication)
> 
> There is essentially **none**. `notes.md:2268-2276` states it plainly:
> ```
> 2268: Nothing is enforced. `users.json` is `{name, phone}` with no authority field,
> 2269: and the only privilege check in the composed source is
> 2270: `overlay.rs`'s `ctx_may_write_layer` — localhost tooling may write the shared
> 2271: layer, a logged-in user may write their own world and nobody else's.
> ...
> 2275: So **the human-supervised builder IS the permission system** ... That holds at two
> 2276: users and fails at a campaign team.
> ```
> The check itself, `features/miso/loop/context/converge/overlay/overlay.rs`:
> ```
> 26:    fn ctx_may_write_layer() -&gt; bool {
> 27:        context_user_now().starts_with("local:")
> 28:    }
> ```
> i.e. **shared-layer write privilege is granted purely by being non-tunnel** (see `per-user.rs:38-56`, which assigns `local:_local` to any cookie-less non-tunnel request). Same single point of failure as the gate.
> 
> Identity binding per request, `features/miso/loop/context/per-user/per-user.rs`:
> ```
> 38:    fn context_user_of(cookie: String, tunnel: bool, query: String) -&gt; String {
> 39:        let token = cookie_token(cookie);
> 40:        if !token.is_empty() &amp;&amp; token_valid(token.clone()) {
> 41:            return format!("phone:{}", token_phone(token));
> 42:        }
> 43:        if tunnel { return String::new(); }
> 48:        let name = query_param(query, "user".to_string());
> 49:        if name.is_empty() { return "local:_local".to_string(); }
> 55:        format!("local:{}", name)
> ```
> Good property: cookie always wins, so `?user=` can never spell a real key. Namespace separation `phone:` vs `local:` is what makes that safe.
> 
> `_from` stamping is server-side and unspoofable, `messaging.rs:40`:
> ```
> 40:        m["_from"] = serde_json::json!(sender_of(r.cookie.clone()));
> ```
> But `overlay.rs:220` deliberately **blanks `_from`** (`anonymised`) before re-dispatch, and `attention.rs:42` then uses *empty `_from`* as the signal that a message came from the builder:
> ```
> 42:            &amp;&amp; m["_from"].as_str().unwrap_or("").is_empty()
> ```
> That's an "absence of identity = elevated identity" pattern worth attacking.
> 
> Historic bug documented in `features/miso/users/whole-number/whole-number.md:20-33`: identity used to be `tag(phone)` = **last 4 digits**, which collided across users and let one person read/overwrite another's data. Fixed by `sender_of` → `phone:+44…`. Note `blackbox.rs:31` **still uses the 4-digit `tag`** for log labelling.

> ## Highest-value red-team targets, ranked
> 
> 1. **`gate.rs:25` `if !r.tunnel { return existing.route(r); }`** — network position, not credentials, is the authorization boundary. Also grants `local:` shared-layer write (`overlay.rs:26-28`) and unrestricted `?user=` context selection.
> 2. **Un-revocable 1-year tokens** (`users.rs:104`, `pin.rs:174-180`) with no guest-list recheck on `token_valid`.
> 3. **Passkey login challenges unbound to a user** + credential-ID enumeration before challenge consumption (`passkey.rs:279, 287-291, 300`).
> 4. **Non-atomic flat-file state under concurrency** — `challenges.txt` (`passkey.rs:90-106`), `pending.txt` (`pin.rs:30-43`), `sends.txt`, `passkeys.txt`, `push-subs.txt`: full read-modify-write with no locking. Concurrent challenge consumption and concurrent PIN-attempt-counter writes are both winnable races (attempt counter reset by racing writes ⇒ unlimited PIN guesses).
> 5. **4-digit modulo-biased PIN** (`pin.rs:11-15`) with no verify-endpoint rate limit.
> 6. **Secrets at mode 0644 with no chmod** (`users.rs:62`, `push.rs:33`) and **Vonage credentials on `curl` argv** (`vonage.rs:21-22`).
> 7. **Guest-list membership oracle** (`pin.rs:96-99`) and no attestation verification (`enrol.login.js:19`).</result>

The sweep came back and it confirms my reads — and it surfaced the thing that actually matters most, which I hadn't yet seen: the gate trusts *network position*, not credentials. That's the load-bearing claim, so I'm verifying it with my own eyes before I put it in front of you.

Confirmed at `gate.rs:25-27`: a request without the tunnel header skips the cookie check and goes straight through to the data routes, and `per-user.rs:43-55` + the overlay check hand that same off-tunnel caller `local:` write rights. So the real authorization boundary is "did this arrive through Cloudflare," set by the `cf-connecting-ip` header in `serve.rs`. Whether that's catastrophic or just a soft spot depends entirely on one thing: what address the server binds. Let me check.

Confirmed the last piece: `serve.rs:25` binds `0.0.0.0:8095`, and `tunnel` is set purely by the presence of a `cf-connecting-ip` header (line 64) — a header the client controls. That's everything I need. Here's my read.

## How secure is miso's auth, really

**Bottom line:** the cryptography is careful and, as far as I can see, correct — this isn't sloppy work. The weakness isn't in the maths, it's in *what the maths is protecting* and *what stands in for a permission system*. For two trusted people on a home network it's fine. As the thing a **campaign** with a separate support person and a confidential supporter list leans on, it isn't there yet — and the code confirms exactly what `notes.md` already admits: "the human-supervised builder IS the permission system… fails at a campaign team."

### What's genuinely solid (so this is fair)
- **The session token is real crypto.** HMAC-SHA256 over `phone.expiry`, signed with a 32-byte urandom secret. You cannot forge a token without the secret. The HMAC is hand-rolled but the ipad/opad construction is right, and comparisons are constant-time.
- **The passkey/WebAuthn login is done properly** — origin check, rpIdHash check, it insists on the user-verified flag (Face ID actually happened), the challenge is single-use, and the ECDSA-P256 signature is verified over the correct `authData ‖ SHA256(clientData)` message. Hand-rolled WebAuthn is usually a bug farm; this one holds up.
- Cookie flags are all set (`Secure`, `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Lax`), the PIN path is rate-limited, and the `phone:` vs `local:` namespace split means a `?user=` parameter can never spell a real person's identity.

### Where it actually breaks, in order of how much it matters for a campaign

**1. The trust boundary is "which network path you came in on," not "who you are."** `gate.rs:25` waves through *any* request that doesn't carry Cloudflare's `cf-connecting-ip` header — no cookie needed — and hands it `local:` write rights to the shared world on top. The server binds `0.0.0.0:8095` (all interfaces), and `tunnel` is decided by a client-supplied header. So the whole login wall rests on one assumption: **nobody can reach the mini's port 8095 except through Cloudflare.** With a Cloudflare *Tunnel* (outbound daemon) the internet probably can't — but anyone on the LAN in the house where the mini lives can, and the day that port gets forwarded, or the app runs somewhere with a public IP, the wall is simply gone. This is the single thing I'd fix first. *The one fact I can't verify from here: whether `185.96.221.52:8095` is actually firewalled. Worth confirming with a port scan from outside.*

**2. One file on the mini is the entire kingdom, and it's mode 0644.** `~/.miso-auth/secret` lets you silently mint a valid year-long cookie for *any* phone on the list — undetectable, and unrevocable short of rotating the secret (which logs everyone out at once). Sitting right next to it, `users.json` *is* the confidential supporter list — names and phone numbers. Anyone who reads that directory once (a backup, the SSH key, physical access to the mini, a foothold on the box) gets both impersonation and the membership list. The good crypto is exactly why this file is the whole game.

**3. SMS is the root of trust, and SMS can't beat a determined adversary.** Every fresh device bootstraps from one SMS code. SIM-swap, SS7, a colluding carrier insider, or just seizing someone's phone → you request a code as them and you're in. No code change fixes this; it's inherent to SMS-as-root. For an ordinary app that's an accepted risk; for a contested local campaign it's the most realistic real-world break.

**4. Tokens are 1-year bearers with no revocation and no guest-list recheck.** `token_valid` checks only signature + expiry. Remove someone from `users.json` — they quit, went hostile, lost their phone — and their cookie keeps working for up to a year. Logout only clears the local cookie. A campaign needs "cut this person off *now*"; today there's no lever short of rotating the secret.

**5. A cluster of concrete code-level cracks**, none catastrophic alone but each worth closing: passkey *login* challenges aren't bound to a user (any live challenge works with any credential); the flat-file stores (`challenges.txt`, `pending.txt`) do read-modify-write with no locking, so concurrent requests can race — including resetting the PIN attempt counter, which turns "3 guesses" into "unlimited"; `auth/request` is a **membership oracle** that returns a supporter's *name* on a hit (403 vs 200), so anyone can enumerate numbers to harvest who's on the list; and the 4-digit PIN is modulo-biased (low codes ~2× as likely).

### The honest summary
Nobody's going to *forge* their way in — the crypto forecloses that. They'll get in by **being on the wrong network, reading one file off the mini, or taking over a supporter's phone number** — and once in, there's essentially no authorization layer to stop them doing anything, because there isn't one yet (only `overlay.rs`'s single localhost check). That's the gap between "works for me and one other person" and "safe for a campaign team with a support person who isn't you." The pieces you'd need — an authority field beside the guest list, revocation, a real ingress boundary — are already sketched in your own notes; the code just hasn't caught up to the threat model yet.

Want me to turn any of these into fixes? The two with the best effort-to-safety ratio are **(a)** binding the origin to localhost + a shared secret header from cloudflared (closes #1 properly), and **(b)** adding a server-side token-version / guest-list recheck so you can actually revoke someone.
